item.title: Executing Isaac Sim Pick-and-Place Tasks Using SimReady Assets and Agent Controls
item.description:
Executing Isaac Sim Pick-and-Place Tasks Using SimReady Assets and Agent Controls

A walkthrough demonstrates a beverage can pick-and-place task in Isaac Sim using the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and AI agent-generated controls. The workflow shows how to compose the scene, verify asset behaviors, and execute automated pick-and-place maneuvers.

🔍 Overview of SimReady Assets

For robotics workflows, a SimReady designation indicates an OpenUSD asset is prepared with properties needed for defined simulation use cases. Key aspects of the asset ecosystem include:

  • SimReady Foundation: Defines the required features an OpenUSD asset needs for a specific simulation use case.
  • SimReady Central: An open asset library hosted on Hugging Face that offers reusable robot and object assets along with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence.
  • Search Endpoints: Allows users to leverage the SimReady Central Space search service endpoint or USD Search endpoint to find OEM-curated content.

⚙️ Component Profiles and Settings

The pick-and-place example utilizes assets with validated simulation properties to establish a shared baseline for asset reuse:

Asset Profile Validated Properties Role in Simulation
UR17G Arm Robot-Body 4.0.0 Passing PhysX driven-joint checks (joint-drive settings) Executes arm movement and positioning
Robotiq 2F-140 Gripper Robot-Gripper 3.0.0 Passing PhysX driven-joint checks (joint-drive settings) Grasps and releases the beverage can
Beverage Can N/A Authored collisions and mass properties Rests on the work surface and serves as target object

🧩 Setup and Task Execution

The simulation workflow integrates scene assembly, system validation, and agent execution:

  • Asset Preparation: Download complete asset folders from SimReady Central (via direct download or Hugging Face CLI) so Isaac Sim can locate supporting files without missing-file errors.
  • Environment Launch: Start Isaac Sim version 6.2 from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled (./isaac-sim.sh --enable isaacsim.code_editor.python_server).
  • Agent Configuration: Set up an agent configured with skills from the Agent Skills documentation. The model—such as GPT-6 Sol—executes Python against Isaac Sim to create and run the task code.
  • Scene & Task Definition: Assemble the work surface, arm-gripper assembly, and initial positions. Review joint limits, confirm the can rests on the surface without falling through, and configure controls to grasp, lift, move, and release the can.

#Robotics #IsaacSim #OpenUSD #SimReady #AIAgents

Source: Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

item.title: FoundationWorlds launches ToyBlocks simulation framework for robot learning
item.description:
FoundationWorlds launches ToyBlocks simulation framework for robot learning

Today a new framework called FoundationWorlds was introduced, pairing a controlled simulated world with tools for automatically generating tasks, training demonstrations, and metrics to measure a robot’s behavior over time.

🔍 Overview

  • The first FoundationWorld is ToyBlocks, an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop.
  • ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations – recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation – without requiring time‑consuming teleoperation.
  • It builds on earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces.

🧩 How it works

  • Skill generation uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning in Isaac Lab, Nvidia’s open‑source framework for robot learning in simulation.
  • Policies learn non‑prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up.
  • Skill generation can draw on privileged information (exact block position and orientation) that a real robot cannot sense, enabling automatic creation of skills that would otherwise need teleoperation.
  • A task‑and‑motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences skills to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them.
  • Each plan run in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations with labels describing the performed task or skill.
  • Data generation scales by running hundreds of plans in parallel on a single GPU, achieving up to 24 × real‑time performance.

⚙️ Key features

  • Designed around four requirements:
    1. Realistic physics and appearance
    2. Automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale
    3. Challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity
    4. Broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain
  • Blocks display pictures and letters, enabling searching, sorting, and arranging tasks.
  • A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs.
  • Domain randomization varies block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene to test generalization.
  • High‑level reasoning models decide what to do; low‑level action models control the robot’s movements.
  • Molmo 2 selects skills (e.g., rotation, flipping) via a pointing interface; ManiFlow executes the commanded skills on the simulated arm.
  • The controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets.

💡 Why it matters

  • ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain, providing realistic physics, automatic data generation, and a blend of reasoning and dexterity challenges.
  • By training models from raw sensor observations, the framework bridges the gap between simulation and real‑world perception problems.

#Robotics #Simulation #MachineLearning #AI

Source: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

item.title: NVIDIA Releases Four Open Cosmos 3‑Nano Checkpoints for Interactive World Simulation
item.description:
NVIDIA Releases Four Open Cosmos 3‑Nano Checkpoints for Interactive World Simulation

NVIDIA has added four open‑weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family, enabling interactive world simulation and multi‑sensor, multi‑view driving scene generation.

🔍 Overview

  • The new checkpoints are built on the Cosmos 3 Nano architecture and each contains 16 B trainable parameters.
  • All models are released under OpenMDW 1.1, which permits both commercial and non‑commercial use.
  • They target
    • offline synthetic driving data creation,
    • fast streaming simulation,
    • text‑guided visual rendering, and
    • bimanual robot interaction.

🧩 How it works

  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Transfer‑Auto generates synchronized video from up to 11 camera views (including fisheyes) and joint RGB‑LiDAR data. It uses per‑camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls for scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance.
  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Auto is a causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer‑Auto. It produces small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in a few denoising steps, leveraging generated history and updated driving controls for long, interactive rollouts. A simulation runtime and WSM renderer are required to update controls from driving inputs.
  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Transfer takes simulator controls and a text prompt to render photorealistic video observations. The physics and ground‑truth state remain with the simulator; the text prompt only influences appearance.
  • Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Bimanual predicts video based on robot or camera actions. It supports two‑arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controllable by a policy or human‑operated joysticks. Training used 59 control values padded to 64, with a schema that defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains.

⚙️ Key details

  • Open weight: All four checkpoints are open‑weight and can be post‑trained on user data to match specific camera layouts, LiDAR configurations, or environments.
  • Multi‑sensor sync: Camera and LiDAR streams are generated together, linking visual observations with 3‑D sensing.
  • Control flexibility: Scene and traffic‑signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, enabling study of driving‑policy responses.
  • Streaming interaction: Streaming generation ties video prediction to ongoing interaction, allowing exploration of how actions and observations unfold together.
  • Licensing: Released under OpenMDW 1.1, allowing commercial and non‑commercial use.

🚀 Availability

The four checkpoints—Cosmos3‑Nano‑Transfer‑Auto, Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Auto, Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Transfer, and Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Bimanual—are now available as open‑weight models in the Cosmos 3 family.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides researchers with open tools for generating realistic driving data across many sensors and viewpoints.
  • Enables fast, interactive simulation of driving scenarios, supporting closed‑loop policy evaluation.
  • Extends simulation capabilities to robotic manipulation with bimanual actions, broadening the scope of world‑model research.
Model Primary capability
Cosmos3‑Nano‑Transfer‑Auto Offline multi‑view driving data generation with weather, lighting, text‑guided appearance, and joint RGB‑LiDAR sync
Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Auto Fast streaming of synchronized camera video and LiDAR for interactive driving rollouts
Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Transfer Convert simulator controls + text prompt into photorealistic video observations
Cosmos3‑Nano‑Sim‑Bimanual Predict video from bimanual robot actions; supports YAM and AgiBot two‑arm embodiments

#NVIDIA #WorldSimulation #OpenModels #AI #LiDAR

Source: New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation

item.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark and Isaac Lab Enable Simulated Navigation Training for Microduck Robot
item.description:
NVIDIA RTX Spark and Isaac Lab Enable Simulated Navigation Training for Microduck Robot

NVIDIA demonstrated an end‑to‑end workflow that uses RTX Spark, Isaac Lab, and Omniverse tools to create a simulated obstacle course, train a navigation policy for the Microduck robot, and evaluate the policy in Isaac Sim.

🔍 Overview

  • Teaching a robot to navigate an obstacle course requires perception, balance, and the ability to adjust actions when obstacles block the path ahead, not just a walking policy.
  • The development process links three stages: creating assets and an environment, using physics simulation to model robot‑environment interaction, and training + evaluating policies in simulation.

🛠️ Tools and Roles

Component Role
RTX Spark Local development hub; supports AI‑assisted planning, policy validation, and receives trained policies for local evaluation in Isaac Sim.
Isaac Lab Cloud‑based robot‑learning framework for reinforcement learning.
Newton Models physical behavior for simulation.
Omniverse libraries Generate simulated visual observations via RTX rendering.
Isaac Sim Runs local evaluation of trained policies returned from RTX Spark.
Hermes Translates prompts into step‑by‑step project plans and creates asset inventories from images.
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt Works with Hermes to generate project plans and analyze images for reusable assets.
Astra Builds and tests assets; directs FreeCAD geometry creation and Blender material application.
SimReady Central Library Free, ungated library of >2,000 simulation‑ready OpenUSD assets.
Microduck Reference quadruped robot used for navigation training.

📐 Workflow Steps

  1. Write a natural‑language prompt that describes the obstacle course and what Microduck must learn.
  2. On RTX Spark, Hermes and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt translate the prompt into a detailed project plan (task, resources, outputs, stages).
  3. Review official Microduck documentation and summarize its capabilities, constraints, and unknowns.
  4. Define the course layout, obstacle dimensions, clearances, and intended route.
  5. Generate a photorealistic concept image using a verified Microduck reference image.
  6. Hermes and Nemotron analyze the concept image, extract unique reusable assets, assign identifiers, and create cropped reference images.
  7. Astra enhances the references, models geometry in FreeCAD, and adds fine details and materials in Blender.
  8. Assemble the assets into a simulated environment; Newton provides physics, Omniverse renders visuals.
  9. Train a navigation policy with Isaac Lab in the cloud using the simulated environment.
  10. Return the trained policy to RTX Spark and evaluate it locally in Isaac Sim.
  11. Verify robot capabilities, test navigation, obstacle handling, and reset logic—all in simulation (no physical hardware).
  12. Package the plan, robot brief, concept, asset inventory, crops, and execution instructions for reproducibility.

📊 What You’ll Learn

  • How to create a simulated obstacle course for a quadruped robot.
  • How AI agents (Hermes, Nemotron, Astra) automate planning, asset extraction, and 3D modeling.
  • How to train a navigation policy with Isaac Lab and validate it with RTX Spark and Isaac Sim.
  • How to leverage the SimReady Central Library for reusable simulation assets.

#NVIDIA #Robotics #Simulation #ReinforcementLearning #AIAgents

Source: Using AI Agents to Teach Robots Like Microduck to Walk in Simulation | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Skild AI launches S1, a video‑to‑robot foundation model for manipulation
item.description:
Skild AI launches S1, a video‑to‑robot foundation model for manipulation

🔍 Overview

Skild AI unveiled S1 in August 2026 as its flagship foundation model for robotic manipulation. The system can learn a new task from a single video demonstration without any additional task‑specific training or weight adjustments.

🧩 How S1 Works

  • The model receives a video showing a task and then attempts to replicate the observed task using a robot, without modifying its weights or requiring a specific post‑training phase.
  • S1 is trained using episodes in which a visual demonstration describes the task to be performed.
  • It learns to relate what it observes in the video to the current scene and the available motor controls, reconstructing an action policy that achieves the same goal with its own robotic body.
  • Pre‑training combines several data types: teleoperation, first‑person human videos, simulation, and experiments conducted on robots.
  • Several scenarios did not appear in the pre‑training data; basic gestures are combined into novel sequences.

📊 Performance Metrics

  • On unseen tasks lasting four to eight minutes, trained on a reported 100,000 hours of data, S1 achieved an average cumulative success rate per step of 66 %, compared with 9 % for a linguistic baseline.
  • The metric aggregates the success rates of the various stages; it does not represent a 66 % success rate for each mission.
  • Human intervention was used to reset the system after a failure so that all stages could be evaluated.
  • A real‑world demonstration is estimated to be equivalent to approximately 380 post‑training sessions on the tasks studied.

🛠️ Supporting Infrastructure

Component Role
Cosmos Organizes and enriches video data
Omniverse Provides virtual environments
Isaac Sim Provides virtual environments
Isaac Lab Used for reinforcement learning
TensorRT Optimizes inference

On September 10 2026 NVIDIA detailed this infrastructure, highlighting how Cosmos, Omniverse, Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, and TensorRT work together to train, simulate, and deploy S1.

🚀 Availability

  • S1 is available through select deployments and partnerships, not as a freely downloadable model.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Enables robots to acquire new manipulation skills from a single video, dramatically reducing the data collection and training time required for each new task.
  • Demonstrated capabilities include repotting a plant, making filter coffee, making pancakes, and assembling a kit, with sequences lasting up to ten minutes and involving several successive gestures.
  • For the repotting task, the company reports that it went from recording the demonstration to beginning autonomous execution in eleven minutes.
  • The same set of weights generates all the examples shown, confirming the model’s ability to generalize across diverse tasks.

#SkildAI #Robotics #FoundationModel #Simulation

Source: 5 Steps to Create SimReady Assets for Robotics with Frontier AI Models | NVIDIA Technical Blog Source: Skild AI’s S1: Learning a Robotic Task from a Video

item.title: Introduction of SimLife Platform and SimLife-BP Behavioral Pattern Benchmark
item.description:
Introduction of SimLife Platform and SimLife-BP Behavioral Pattern Benchmark

Researchers have introduced SimLife, a scalable platform designed to simulate long-term household life, alongside a corresponding benchmark called SimLife-BP to evaluate long-context pattern understanding.

🔍 Overview

SimLife is a simulation platform that provides:

  • Rich visual observations
  • Ground-truth action logs
  • Synthetic dialogues with audio

⚙️ Key details

SimLife-BP is used to evaluate the ability to infer latent behavioral rules from observations spanning weeks or months. The benchmark consists of:

  • 106 episodes
  • 1,439 question-answer pairs
  • Average episode length of 15.49 hours and 38.57 in-game days

🧩 How it works

Tasks within the benchmark probe the following types of reasoning under various levels of rule hints:

  • Direct reasoning
  • Counterfactual reasoning
  • Noisy reasoning
  • Inverse reasoning

💡 Why it matters

Evaluations of frontier models and architectures revealed several limitations in current AI capabilities:

  • Models often achieve surface-level prediction instead of comprehensive rule understanding.
  • Models rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning based on evidence.
  • Models struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change.

#SimLife #AIbenchmarks #LongContext #BehavioralModeling

Source: SIMLIFE: Pattern Understanding for Long-Horizon Human-Agent Partnership
